What the redesign changed

Thirty-one screens of the property suite, before and after the navy / gold rebuild — same database, same frame, minutes apart — with the numbers underneath.

How this was made

The old code was checked out into a separate worktree and served alongside the current app, both pointed at the same copy of the database. Every pair is the same URL in the same 1440 × 900 frame, light theme, minutes apart. Nothing was staged for the photographs — where a panel is empty, that building really has no photos. The four pages that returned 404 against the old code are the four that did not exist yet.

Getting in

Sign in

The form floated on the bare page ground; it sits in a card now, on a gold-gradient button, with the reset link live instead of grey and inert. The bigger change is invisible: sign-in was a standalone document with its own palette, fonts and field CSS — a different gold and a different navy from the app it signs you into, and no working dark mode. It loads the shared stylesheet now. Photo, scrim and gold bloom kept on purpose.

The shell

Dashboard

Seven light nav groups became three on navy — the single change that does most of the work. The import/export banner gave way to a collection figure and a “needs your attention” panel, and the bell top-right now carries a live count instead of being an ornament.

Portfolio

Buildings — list

carried by the system

Unchanged as a page. Included because not everything needed rebuilding.

Buildings — cards

The card view gained the two figures the handoff leads a property with: an occupancy pill on the photo, net per month beside the unit count. Zero pills before, four after — and the arithmetic was already being computed for the mobile card, so the desktop simply started using it.

Building detail

The only page in the app loading Bootstrap from a CDN, which is why it read as a different product. Now on the system: identity band, tabs with counts, occupancy and agreement rings, and a real empty state per panel. Shown on a near-empty building deliberately — one unit, no photos — because that is where empty states hold or fall apart.

Units

Thirteen columns down to eight — the column wall is visible on the left. Land Lord, Condition, Deposit, Elec. A/c and View were each checked present on the unit’s own page before removal, so this is a move, not a loss. Area and rent moved onto the shared numeric cell, and the horizontal scrollbar went with them.

Tenants

Every old column was identity — type, ID/CR, email, nationality — and none of it about the tenancy. It leads with unit, lease end, outstanding balance and status now: what someone scanning a tenant list is actually after. Identity stayed on the profile the row opens.

Operations

Maintenance

The largest single change. A filtered table became a board: seven statuses collapsed into three columns by who holds the work, oldest first, anything sitting over a fortnight called out. The table is still there behind a toggle, because a board cannot sort, filter or paginate — and both read the same filtered query.

Maintenance request

carried by the system

Where a board card opens to.

Reports

A three-up grid became a four-up library with an explicit action per card, one array now driving both the mobile and desktop lists so they cannot drift. The handoff’s “recent exports” panel is deliberately absent — nothing recorded an export, so there was nothing truthful to put in it.

Administration

Users

Bound to the new Roles page by a shared tab bar rather than merged with it: a fifteen-row capability matrix inside a filtered, paginated user table would bury both.

Activity feed

It recorded record changes only, so a brute-force attempt would have left no trace. Sign-ins, sign-outs, failed attempts, lockouts, password resets and profile edits all reach it now, with two tiles that count them.

Pages that did not exist before

No “before” to show — these returned 404 against the 17 August code.

Roles & Permissions

new

The sidebar carried an entry that rendered dimmed and inert. It resolves now — to a reference, not a form: there is no roles table and no permissions table, so rather than fake an editable matrix it shows every gate that exists and names the code enforcing it.

Your profile

new

The users resource is admin-only, so a User or Maintenance account could not change even its own name, email or password. Role is shown and deliberately not editable.

Password reset

new

There was no route for it at all. A locked-out account could only be recovered by an administrator, which stopped being acceptable once sign-in gained a lockout.

Branding

new

Site name, logo and favicon, so the suite can be re-skinned without editing files on the server.

What was added, not just restyled

Roughly half of this work was not visual. These are things the app could not do on 17 August.

Sign-in rate limiting

Five attempts per identifier and IP, twenty per IP across all identifiers, so rotating usernames still trips a limit. The form previously accepted unlimited password guesses.

Authentication in the audit log

Signed in, signed out, failed attempt, lockout — none of which were recorded before.

Password reset by email

No route existed. Recovery meant asking an administrator.

Your own profile

Self-service name, email and password for every role, with role left to administrators.

Account menu

The user chip was a submit button for the logout form while showing a chevron that promised a menu. One stray click ended the session.

Notification bell

A dead button became a live feed of overdue invoices, leases ending and requests awaiting a decision.

Record search on ⌘K

The palette filtered a hardcoded list while the top bar advertised searching buildings, tenants and units. It searches records now, server-side and role-gated.

Lease-expiry watch

Nothing watched it; a lease could run out with no warning. A weekly digest now tells the staff and records the run even when mail fails.

Maintenance board

Work grouped by the stage it is at, alongside the table rather than replacing it.

Recoverable deletes, groundwork

Deletes are still permanent, but the schema is in place: deleted_at on thirteen tables with eleven unique business codes rebuilt as partial indexes, so a trashed record cannot block its own replacement.

Worth knowing

  • Two endpoints compared: 4aba943 (17 Aug) against the current branch head. Things broke and were fixed in between — the Reports cards, for one, lost their padding in the interim commits and got it back.
  • Every frame is 1440 × 900, light theme, half pixel density, both versions served from the same copy of the database minutes apart. Landscape and above-the-fold on purpose, so the pairs are comparable; a few changes sit below the visible area.
  • Pages marked carried by the system had no page-specific work. They look different because the shell and the shared components changed underneath them — which is the argument for having a shared system at all.
  • One fault found on the way was invisible rather than ugly: the content column is a flex column, so any section taller than the viewport was shrunk and clipped instead of scrolling — 1,024px of the roles matrix and 332px of the invoices table were in the page, laid out, and unreachable.
  • None of this is pushed. Seventeen commits sit on feature/navy-gold-building-detail with no upstream, and the staging box has been running the working tree directly.
